title: The Drowned Bell
subtitle: Carrow Island, Penobscot Bay, Maine, October to November 1924

listing.title: The Drowned Bell 🌊
listing.blurb: Maine, October 1924. Fifty-three years ago a gale took Carrow Island's old church into the sea, bell and all. This summer the bell began to ring again, under the water, at the lowest tides, and each time it rings someone on the island gets up and walks into the sea. You come out on the mail boat through the fog: a folklorist, an insurance man, a doctor whose sister was the last one taken, a bootlegger with a crate to hide. The island has kept its secret for half a century and it has its reasons. The tide is the clock. Levels 3–6.

synopsis: Carrow Island lies eighteen miles out from Rockland at the mouth of Penobscot Bay: three miles of spruce and granite, a harbor village of a hundred and forty people, a lighthouse on the seaward head, a cemetery on the hill, and, on the island's southern shore, a long low spit called Church Point that runs out across a gravel bar to nothing. Until October 1871 the island's Union Church stood at the end of it. In the gale of 18 October 1871 the sea came over the Bar, undermined the Point, and took the church down onto the ledge beyond, the Church Shelf, where it lies to this day in four fathoms, its belfry eight feet under at an ordinary low water. The island's history, the Proprietors' Record kept by the five old families who own the wharf, the store and most of the land, says that twenty-three people who had sheltered in the church were lost with it. That is true. It is not the whole truth. They had not sheltered there. They had been shut in, and the doors spiked with iron, by order of the island's five Proprietors, because they were sick with a fever the island feared more than the sea, and when the gale tide came over the Bar the five men stood on the shore with lanterns and listened to the bell ring for four hours, and did not go. The minister's wife, Ardelia Vining, who had gone in to nurse them, rang it until the church went down. For fifty-two years afterwards the island's sexton, Zebulon Lunt, whose parents were among the dead, climbed the new church tower at the lowest night low water of every spring tide and rang the bell by hand, under a bequest nobody remembered the reason for. Zeb Lunt died in June 1924. In July the new young minister stopped the ringing. On the night of 1 August, at low water, the island heard a bell ringing under the sea off Church Point, and an old fisherman named Enoch Farr got up from his supper table, walked down to the shore and out into the water, and was not seen again. Since then the drowned bell has rung four more times, at the bottom of each spring tide: two more people have walked into the sea and not come back, two others were called and held back, and one of those has since vanished. Every one of them was of the blood of the five Proprietors. The party come out to Carrow on the mail boat on Friday 10 October 1924, in fog, with a recast church bell in a crate in the hold: a folklorist after a ballad, an insurance investigator with three claims and no bodies, a doctor whose sister was taken on 15 September, a bootlegger whose whisky is packed in the straw around the bell, a new assistant lighthouse keeper, a stage medium hired for a seance. The campaign runs by the tide. On 14 October the bell rings again, and the party learn its first rules: when it rings, whom it calls, and how it can be answered. On 29 October comes the lowest tide in a hundred years, and for one hour before dawn the drowned church stands bare on the Shelf with the sea drawn back from it: walkable, open to whoever dares, and calling every one of the Proprietors' blood out across the flats at once. Three days later the All Saints' gale cuts the island off, the dead come ashore on the flood tides, and the town turns on the strangers. And on 13 November, at the next spring low, the island must decide whether to say aloud what the five families did, and ring the bell once for each of the people they left in the dark. The bell is not evil. It is still calling for help. The rules are fair, the clues are there, and the families have reasons a decent person can understand. What they owe is still owed.
hook: The Rockland wharf, Friday 10 October 1924, seven in the morning. The mail boat Viola R., forty-six feet, a Knox County mail contract, a one-lung engine and Captain Solon Stinson, leaves for Carrow Island three days a week, weather permitting, and today the weather does not permit much: a flat grey calm and a fog bank sitting on the bay like wet wool. Stinson takes the mail sacks, the freight and you, and asks no questions, because the only freight anyone has wanted to send to Carrow this autumn is coffins without anyone to put in them. In the hold there is a crate eight feet long, stencilled UNION CHURCH, CARROW ISLAND, ME. HANDLE WITH CARE, with a recast church bell in it, and something in the straw around the bell that clinks. On deck there are six of you who have never met and have each, separately, decided to go to an island that nobody on the Rockland waterfront will talk about. Halfway out the fog closes in completely. Stinson throttles down to steerage and steers by the compass and the sound of the Carrow Head fog bell, slow and regular as a heartbeat, off to the east. And then, for a few seconds, everyone on deck hears another bell: deeper, muffled, coming up through the planking under their feet, as if it were ringing somewhere under the sea. Stinson does not slow down. 'Tide's not right for her,' he says, to nobody in particular. 'She only rings on the big tides. You'll be hearing things. Everybody does, first time.' He does not look at any of you. The fog opens on a granite wharf, a row of white houses and a church with an empty belfry, and a small crowd of islanders waiting for the mail, who watch you come ashore in a silence you can hear.

setting.name: Carrow Island, Penobscot Bay, Maine, 10 October to 14 November 1924
setting.description: Carrow Island, Carrow Harbor and everyone on them are fictional; the coast, the year and the history are real. Maine has been dry since 1851 and the whole country since 1920, and the Maine coast, with its thousands of islands, coves and fog banks and Canada a day's run away, is one of the great smuggling coasts of Prohibition: Canadian and French schooners from Nova Scotia and Saint-Pierre lie at anchor beyond the twelve-mile line on Rum Row, fast lobster boats with aircraft engines run cases ashore at night, and the Coast Guard's patrol boats are too few and too slow. The fishing that built the islands is failing; the granite quarries that boomed in the 1870s and 1880s are closed; island populations are half what they were. Carrow had four hundred people in 1871, when it had a granite quarry, a fish-curing works and forty schooners; it has a hundred and forty now, a lobster fishery, a few herring weirs, a summer cottage or two, and, since 1921, a share in the rum trade that keeps the store open and the young men home. Carrow Harbor is the only village: a granite wharf, the Proprietors' Store (store, post office and the island's one telephone, on a submarine cable laid in 1916), the white Union Church built in 1873 with its tower and, since August, no bell, a one-room school, the Grange hall, and forty houses up the slope. The Captain's House, Orpha Sprague's, stands highest. Behind the village Spruce Hill rises to the Burying Ground. The island's eastern end is Carrow Head, a granite bluff with Carrow Head Light, a white cast-iron tower of 1857, the keeper's house, the oil house and a fog bell in a wooden frame. On the north side, out of sight of the village, is Sculpin Cove, with Galen Coombs's fish house and wharf and the fast boats. On the south side Church Point runs out across the Bar, a gravel spit that floods at high water, to the cellar holes of the old Point settlement, and beyond it, under the sea, lies the Church Shelf and the drowned Union Church of 1858. The mainland is eighteen miles off: Rockland, the county seat, with its lime kilns, sardine factories, the Knox County courthouse and the Mariner, a weekly newspaper whose files go back to the 1840s.
setting.atmosphere: Fog, tide, granite and cold water. The bay is never quiet: gulls, the slap of water on the wharf, a bell buoy groaning off the ledges, a one-lung engine putting across the harbor before light, the fog bell at the Head striking every twenty seconds through a thick night. The light at the Head sweeps the fog every ten seconds and turns it white. Late October smells of rockweed, wood smoke, bait barrels, kerosene and wet spruce, and the days are short: dark by five, cold by six, and the low tides come in the dark. Let the tide be felt in every scene: the harbor drains to mud and fills again twice a day, the Bar is a road at low water and a channel at high, weed hangs on the wharf pilings to show where the water was, and everyone on the island knows what the tide is doing without looking. The islanders are not monsters and must never be played as backward or sinister: they are hard-working, dry-humored, close-mouthed Yankee fishing people who have been carrying a weight for fifty-three years that they did not make, and many of them do not know exactly what it is. They are frightened for their families, ashamed of something they half know, and angry at strangers who come to stare. The horror is quiet until it is not: a bell under the water, a neighbor standing at the tide line in her nightgown with her eyes open, wet footprints coming up from the sea to a door. Dread before gore; the sea does the rest. The bell's call is a compulsion, like hearing your own name called across a field in your mother's voice: the called are not sad and do not want to die; they are answering, and they walk.

regions.name: Carrow Harbor
regions.description: The village around the harbor on the island's west side, facing the mainland. The granite wharf where the mail boat ties up; the Proprietors' Store, kept by First Selectman Ellery Wyman, with the post office window, the telephone on the wall, the tide table nailed beside it, a stove with a ring of chairs, and the island's account books; the Union Church of 1873 with its square tower and its empty bell frame, and the parsonage where the Reverend Kingsley Trask lives alone; the one-room school; the Grange hall, where town meeting is held; forty frame houses up the slope, nearly every one with an iron spike or a horseshoe nailed over the door, an island custom nobody explains. Highest on the hill, the Captain's House, square and white with a widow's walk, where Orpha Sprague, seventy-three, has lived since she was born.

regions.name: Carrow Head and the Light
regions.description: The island's eastern bluff, a mile and a half from the village by a cart road through the spruce. Carrow Head Light, a white cast-iron tower forty feet high on the granite, with a fourth-order lens and a kerosene vapor lamp; the keeper's double house; the oil house; the boat slip; and the fog bell, a thousand-pound bell in a wooden frame struck by a clockwork machine that must be wound every four hours in thick weather. Head keeper Oren Pinkham, sixty-one, has kept the light since 1897; his father Nehemiah kept it before him, from 1868. The station's logbooks, by Lighthouse Service regulation, go back to its first night.

regions.name: Church Point, the Bar and the Shelf
regions.description: The island's southern shore. Church Point is a low grassy spit with the cellar holes of the old Point settlement, a dozen fishermen's houses that stood there until 1871, an old well capped with a granite slab, and a fallen stone wall. It is joined to the island by the Bar, a ridge of gravel and cobble three hundred yards long that is dry for four hours either side of low water and covered at high. At the Point's end the land stops in a raw slope of clay and stone where the church went down. Beyond it the Church Shelf, a broad ledge of granite, slopes out under the water, and on it, in four fathoms at high water and eight feet at an ordinary low, lies the drowned Union Church of 1858, roof broken, tower leaning, with the bell still in it. Galen Coombs's men sink their whisky in salt-weighted sacks on the Shelf's edge; the sacks come up when the salt melts. At the lowest tide in a hundred years the Shelf will be bare.

regions.name: Sculpin Cove and the Outer Water
regions.description: Sculpin Cove, a deep narrow cove on the north shore hidden from the village and the Head, is Galen Coombs's: a fish house on pilings, a wharf, a marine railway, two fast lobster boats with aircraft engines, the Ruth & Ida and the Lark's Daughter, and a crowd of young island men who earn more in a night than their fathers did in a month. Two miles east, the bare ledge called Little Shag, with sheep on it, gives a lee where the Saint-Pierre schooner Bonne Chance anchors on dark nights to land cases. Eighteen miles west is Rockland and the mainland: the mail boat's run, the telephone's cable, and the Coast Guard station.

campaignRules.name: The Tide Clock
campaignRules.description: The campaign runs on the tide and the calendar, from Friday 10 October to Friday 14 November 1924, and the bell keeps its own time whether or not the players are watching. Keep the tide table open (times are Eastern Standard Time, Carrow Harbor) and tell the players what the tide is doing as you would tell them the weather. Twice a day the sea rises about ten feet and falls again; the Bar to Church Point is dry for four hours either side of low water. The bell rings once each spring tide, at the lowest night low water of that spring. THE RINGINGS SO FAR (all fixed history): Fri 1 Aug (Enoch Farr, 66, walked into the sea); Sat 16 Aug (Peleg Sprague rang the church bell by hand in secret; Sophronia Coombs, 40, was found at dawn standing at the tide line, alive); Sun 31 Aug (Clyde Tibbetts, 34, was called and held by his wife Verna until the tide turned; on 2 Sept he staged his own disappearance); Mon 15 Sept (Esther Thurlow, 33, of Boston, taken); Tue 30 Sept (Ellery Wyman ran the lighthouse fog bell's clockwork through the low water; his brother Jotham, 45, was taken anyway). THE CLOCK: db-scenario-001, Fri 10 to Thu 16 Oct; the spring low on Tue 14 Oct at 6:21 p.m. (dark since five) is the next ringing. Between scenarios the GM summarises the days and lets each player choose one or two things to do: a trip to Rockland on the mail boat (it leaves Rockland at seven on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays and starts back from Carrow at one, so a trip ashore means a night or two away), the Mariner's files, the Knox County registry of deeds, a talk with someone who will not talk on the island. db-scenario-002, Fri 17 to Wed 29 Oct: the new moon is 28 Oct, the moon at perigee the same week, and from 26 Oct a three-day northwest gale blows the water out of the bay; the dawn low water on Wed 29 Oct at 5:48 a.m. is the lowest tide in a hundred years, and the Church Shelf is bare from about 5:15 to 6:15. db-scenario-003, Sat 1 to Tue 4 Nov: the All Saints' gale backs into the southeast on the night of 31 Oct and blows for three days; storm tides at about 11:40 a.m. and midnight each day run four feet above the highest the island has seen; the mail boat cannot run, and the telephone cable parts on 1 Nov. db-scenario-004, Wed 5 to Fri 14 Nov: the full moon is 12 Nov; the spring low water on Thu 13 Nov at 6:04 p.m. is the next ringing and the island's last chance before winter. IF NOBODY INTERFERES: 14 Oct, Peleg Sprague walks into the sea; 29 Oct, sixty-one people of the Proprietors' blood walk out across the bare Shelf toward the church and the tide comes back over them, and Galen Coombs's dynamite brings the church's west wall down on the doors; 1 to 3 Nov, the island tears itself apart over the strangers; 13 Nov, the bell rings and calls one more, and goes on ringing every spring tide for as long as there is anyone of the blood left on Carrow.

campaignRules.name: The Bell's Rules (GM only)
campaignRules.description: The drowned bell and the twenty-three dead it rings for follow rules, and the GM never changes them once the players have learned one. The players discover them by investigation (three clues or more to each; see controlFile.clues). RULE 1, WHEN IT RINGS: once each spring tide, at the lowest night low water of that spring, a day or two after the full or the new moon, and for as long as the water is low; never by day, never on the neap tides. RULE 2, WHOM IT CALLS: only those of the blood of the five Proprietors who signed the order and spiked the doors in 1871, Sprague, Wyman, Coombs, Farr and Tibbetts, by birth on either side, wherever they were born, and only the grown: the bell has never called a child and never will; one each ringing, the nearest to the Point, who hears the bell as their own family name being called; except on a tide when the Shelf is bare, when it calls all of them at once. Nobody else is ever called, though anyone can hear the bell. RULE 3, THE ANSWER: a bell rung on Carrow by a living hand, for as long as the drowned bell rings, quiets it for that tide: it was ringing for someone to come, and someone has answered. A machine does not count; a ship's bell rung on a boat at sea does not count. And a called person who is held back from the water, by force or by love, until the tide turns comes back to themselves, cold and shaking and remembering their name in the bell. RULE 4, IRON: the dead cannot pass iron set in place by a living hand. Iron spikes held them in the church for fifty-three years; an iron spike or horseshoe nailed over a door, or an unbroken iron chain across a threshold, keeps them out of a house. The cast-iron tower of the Light is proof against them. Iron weapons hurt them as they would hurt the living (no resistance). RULE 5, REST: the dead rest, and the bell falls silent for good, when the doors of the church have been opened from the outside by a living hand, and the bell has been rung by a hand of the five Proprietors' blood once for each of the dead, as each name is spoken aloud before the people of the island. Wrong rites do nothing, and the dead know you tried: salt, holy water, prayers for the drowned, a wreath on the water, a medal, a hymn, or dynamite, which breaks the church and buries the doors and makes the next ringing call two instead of one. What it wants is what it wanted in 1871: for someone to come.

campaignRules.name: Dread on Carrow Island
campaignRules.description: Use the Horror ruleset's fear checks and Dread (dread.json): a Wisdom saving throw against DC 10 for the sign of it, 15 for seeing it, 20 for the truth of it; failure gains 1 Dread, a natural 1 gains 2; the same horror costs Dread once per scene; knowing one of the bell's rules (above) lowers the DC by 2. This campaign's horrors, by DC. 10: the bell heard faintly under the water; wet footprints coming up from the sea; a cold spot in a Point cellar hole; a name scratched in old plaster. 15: seeing someone walk into the sea with their eyes open; the drowned church rising out of the dark water; the taken sitting in the pews; a Drowned One at the window, or at the door, knocking. 20: hearing your own family name in the bell; reading the Proprietors' order with the five signatures; Ardelia Vining's face. Recovery is the ruleset's, and on Carrow a mug of coffee at the Store stove with company, a hymn in the Union Church, a slug of Galen Coombs's whisky or a joke at Oren Pinkham's kitchen table each count as the once-a-day comfort. Laying the bell at the end drops everyone present to 0. The light goes out at the worst moment once per scenario, not more: the lantern on the Shelf, the vapor lamp in the tower in the storm. Table safety: at the first session the GM asks what the players do not want in the game and honors any player's 'skip that' at once, without question, by cutting away. The call to the sea is a compulsion, an answer to a name, and the GM must always describe it that way and never as a wish to die; no child is ever called, harmed or present at any of the dangerous scenes.

campaignRules.name: Rites That Work
campaignRules.description: Rites on Carrow work only because the bell's rules say so, and anyone can perform them; an Occultist does them better (advantage, from Old Lore). THE ANSWERING: ring a bell on the island by hand for as long as the drowned bell rings, about the twenty minutes either side of the low water. The Union Church bell (the recast one in the crate, once hung: three hours' work and a Mechanics or Athletics check DC 12 with block and tackle, or a desperate improvised frame) is best; a ship's bell on the wharf, a school handbell or the lighthouse fog bell struck by hand (not by its clockwork) all serve. The ringer must keep ringing: a Constitution save DC 10 every five minutes, rising by 2 each time; a second ringer can take over. Each answered ringing quiets the bell for that tide only. HOLDING THE CALLED: a called person walks toward the water at walking pace and fights anyone who stops them with a strength they do not have (treat as a contested Athletics check each round, the called at +4, but they never try to hurt anyone); hold them until the tide turns, about twenty minutes after low water, and they come back. Tying them, locking them in, or sitting on them all work; an unlocked window does not. IRON: an iron spike, nail or horseshoe over a door, or an iron chain across a threshold, set by a living hand, keeps the Drowned out (they stand outside and knock); one already there counts. OPENING THE DOORS: only possible when the Shelf is bare (29 Oct) or by a diver in the deep-sea dress from Sculpin Cove's salvage gear (db-scenario-004 fallback): the double west doors are spiked shut with eight iron spikes; drawing them takes a crowbar and an Athletics check DC 14 per two spikes, or dynamite, which is the wrong rite. THE NAMING: the bell, raised or reached, rung by a hand of the five families' blood once for each of the dead (twenty-three for 1871; Asahel Wyman, whom the bell took in November 1871; Philena Farr in 1898; Enoch Farr, Esther Thurlow and Jotham Wyman in 1924: twenty-eight strokes, and one more for anyone taken since), each name spoken aloud before the people of the island. The names are in three places at least (see controlFile.clues F). A wrong rite costs the performer a fear check DC 15 as the bell answers it with a single stroke under the sea.

campaignRules.name: Standing on Carrow
campaignRules.description: The island watches the strangers and decides about them together, over the Store stove. Track a single Standing score for the party, from -3 (the island wants you gone and will help put you on the boat) to +3 (the island trusts you with its boats and its secret), starting at 0, openly. It rises for saving an islander from the sea (+1), helping haul a boat or a trap line, keeping your mouth shut in Rockland, going to church, standing a watch, telling the truth when it costs you; it falls for prying at funerals, telling the Mariner anything (-1), bringing the Coast Guard or a Prohibition agent to the island (-2), insulting the dead, or being seen at Sculpin Cove by the wrong people. At +2 Orpha Sprague will see the party; at -2 Ellery Wyman will not sell them kerosene; at -3 in the storm (db-scenario-003) the town tries to shut the strangers in the fish house 'until the boat runs', which is the island about to repeat itself. Galen Coombs keeps his own score: he likes anyone who keeps away from his business and is useful to him, and will do anything to anyone who brings the law.

wildernessStarts.label: Carrow Harbor: the mail boat ties up in the fog, Friday morning
Carrow Head Light: the keeper's kitchen, the logbooks on the table
Church Point: the Bar at dusk, the tide going out
Sculpin Cove: a lantern in the fish house, a boat coming in without lights

explorationRules: Carrow is a small island and the map is a schematic of it: the Harbor on the west facing the mainland, the Captain's House above it, Spruce Hill and the Burying Ground behind, the cart road east through the spruce to Carrow Head Light, Sculpin Cove hidden on the north shore, Church Point and the Bar on the south with the Church Shelf beyond, Little Shag offshore to the east, and the mail-boat run to Rockland eighteen miles west. Nowhere on the island is more than forty minutes' walk from anywhere else; in fog it is twice that, and the fog bell at the Head is how you find your way. The unit of time is the tide: six hours from high to low, and the players should always know which way it is going, because the Bar, the Point, the Shelf, the harbor mud and the bell all depend on it. The Tide Clock (campaignRules) is the engine, and the bell keeps it whether or not the party is ready. Run each scenario as a set of named places with islanders who each know a piece of the truth and have a reason not to say it. Nobody is omniscient: Orpha Sprague knows nearly everything and has told no one in fifty-three years; Ellery Wyman knows the families did something and not what; Galen Coombs knows the Shelf better than anyone alive and thinks the bell is a curse to be blown up; most islanders know only that there is iron over every door and you do not go out to the Point on the big tides. The mystery follows the three-clue rule (controlFile.clues). Fights are rare, short and frightening; most scenes are a kitchen table, a store stove, a wet wharf at night, or a voice in the fog. Getting off the island is always possible until the storm, and running away from the Drowned is often the right call. Let the island breathe between horrors: a lobster boat going out at four in the morning, gulls on the wharf, the smell of bait and coffee, a fiddle at the Grange on Saturday, women hanging washing in a north wind, the light sweeping the fog. Money is 1924 dollars: a lobster brings forty cents a pound in Rockland, a lobsterman clears $900 in a good year, a case of Canadian whisky costs $14 on Rum Row and sells for $60 in Portland, a night running cases pays a young island deckhand $50, passage on the mail boat is $1, a room at the Rockland hotel $2.50, and Merrymeeting Life will pay $3,000 on Esther Thurlow if there is a body or a year and a day. The players should come away remembering the sound of that bell, and the faces of the islanders who had to decide whether to say what was done.

controlFile.note: The fixed truth of the campaign, for the GM only. Like a creature's rules, it does not change because a player has a more exciting theory. Carrow Island, Carrow Harbor, Church Point, the Church Shelf, Sculpin Cove, Little Shag, the Union Church, the Proprietors, the Merrymeeting Life & Casualty Company, the Ricker Bell Foundry, the mail boat Viola R., the schooner Bonne Chance and every person in the campaign are fictional. Penobscot Bay, Rockland, Knox County, the Lighthouse Service, Prohibition and Rum Row, the Coast Guard's rum patrol, Maine's town boards of health and their quarantine powers in the 1870s, typhoid fever and the granite and fishing history of the Maine islands are real; no real person appears.
controlFile.theTruth: In September 1871 typhoid fever broke out among the tenant fishing families of Church Point, the dozen poor households who rented their houses, net stands and drying flakes from the island's five Proprietor families, Sprague, Wyman, Coombs, Farr and Tibbetts, who owned the wharf, the store, the fish-curing works and most of the land. The cause was the Point's own well, fouled by the curing works' offal pit uphill of it, which the Proprietors had been asked to move in 1869 and had not. Nobody in 1871 knew that typhoid comes from the water and not from the breath; what the island knew was that a fever had killed eleven people on an island down the bay two years before. On 30 September the schooner Hannah Leighton of Gloucester put into Carrow with two of her crew of six sick. On 9 October the island's board of health, which was the five Proprietors sitting as selectmen, Captain Hezekiah Sprague, Seth Wyman, Jabez Coombs, Reuben Farr and Eliphalet Tibbetts, ordered every sick person and anyone who had nursed them into the Union Church on the Point, the building furthest from the village, and set a watch on the Bar. Ardelia Vining, thirty-four, the minister's wife, went in to nurse them; so did three Point women; so did two well men who would not leave their wives. The minister, the Reverend Joel Vining, was on the mainland at the conference in Bangor. On 14 October one of the Gloucester men, delirious, broke out and walked to the Harbor asking for water, and the five men, frightened, took him back and spiked the church's west doors shut with eight iron spikes from the curing works, and boarded the windows. Food and water were passed in through the vestry window, which was too small to climb through. On the night of 18 October 1871 a southeast gale drove a storm tide over the Bar and around the Point. The sea came into the church. At about eleven o'clock the bell began to ring: Ardelia Vining, in the vestibule, on the bell rope, ringing for help. The five Proprietors came down to the Bar with lanterns; Hezekiah Sprague's daughter Orpha, twenty, held his. The church was a hundred yards across water waist-deep and running; a dory could have reached it, and two of the Point men's grown sons begged to take one. Hezekiah Sprague said no: the fever was in there, and the island's children were not. The other four agreed. They stood on the shore for four hours and forty minutes and listened to the bell, and at twenty minutes to four in the morning the Point slumped into the sea and the church slid off it down onto the Shelf, still ringing, and stopped. Twenty-three people died: Ardelia Vining; Thomas and Rhoda Grindle; Enos and Keziah Lunt; Daniel and Lovina Pressey; Ruel Hupper and his sister Huldah; Nathaniel and Tryphena Kenniston; Oakes and Bethia Ulmer; Joseph Philbrook; Dorcas Wheaton; Jerusha Spurling; Samuel Dolliver; and the Hannah Leighton's crew, Captain John Staples, Patrick Hamor, Antone Joyce, Gustavus Pert, William Torrey and Elias Dunbar. All were adults. The Proprietors' Record of the Gale, written by Seth Wyman, says the twenty-three 'had sheltered in the Point meeting house and were lost with it'. The order of 9 October, with the five signatures and the twenty-three names, Hezekiah Sprague kept in the family Bible, and Orpha Sprague has it now. Afterwards the Point's leases, net stands and fishing privileges, whose holders were dead, passed to the Proprietors through the probate court and unpaid rents. When Joel Vining came home and learned the truth from Orpha, who could not keep it, he did not expose the five; he was a gentle man with no proof but a frightened young woman's word, and the island needed the five. But at the next spring tide, in November 1871, he heard the bell ring under the sea at low water, and saw Seth Wyman's brother Asahel walk into it, and at the spring tide after that he climbed the half-built tower of the new church and rang its bell by hand at the low water, and nobody walked. He worked out three of the bell's rules that winter, wrote them to his brother in Bangor, left a bequest of $400 to pay a sexton to ring 'at the lowest night low water of every spring tide, by hand, so long as the old bell shall ring under the sea', and left the island in 1873. Zebulon Lunt, whose parents Enos and Keziah were in the church, came home from the Grand Banks to find them gone, took the bequest, and rang for fifty-two years. He missed one tide, in March 1898, when he had pneumonia, and Philena Farr walked into the sea. He died in June 1924. In July the new minister, Kingsley Trask, stopped the ringing because nobody would tell him why it was done and it woke the island at all hours; he asked the First Selectman, Ellery Wyman, who knew only that the families had always paid the sexton, and who said 'do as you think best'. Peleg Sprague, Orpha's great-grandson, rang the church bell secretly on 16 August, because Orpha told him to, and it worked; on 20 August the church bell, cracked since the spring, went to the Ricker foundry in East Boston to be recast, by a subscription Trask had raised, and it is in the crate on the party's mail boat. The bell does not hate anyone. The twenty-three dead are still in the dark on the Shelf, behind iron, and the bell is still ringing for someone to come, and it calls the blood of the men who did not. Those it calls walk to the water to answer it, and the sea does the rest; their bodies go to the church, and sit in its pews.
suspects: Orpha Sprague, 73, the oldest person on Carrow, Peleg's great-grandmother: the last living witness of 18 October 1871. She held the lantern. She keeps the order of 9 October in the family Bible and the knowledge of what it means in a silence of fifty-three years. She is not a villain. She loved her father, and she has spent her life being kind to the Point families' descendants in small ways that do not cost the truth. She fears that speaking will destroy the island's families and the island with them; she fears more, now, that not speaking will drown them one by one. She will speak only when she sees that it is the only way, and only to people who have earned it.

Ellery Wyman, 58, First Selectman, keeper of the Proprietors' Store and the island's account books: the families' public face. He knows the families paid the sexton for fifty-two years and that the iron over the doors is not a joke; he does not know what was done. He told Trask to do as he thought best and his brother Jotham walked into the sea on 30 September. He is grieving, guilty and furious, and he will do anything to keep strangers from making the island a newspaper story: in the storm he leads the town against them.

Galen Coombs, 38, Navy veteran, the island's rum-runner: runs Sculpin Cove, two fast boats, a crowd of young men and a deal with the Saint-Pierre schooner Bonne Chance; sinks his cargo in salt-sacks on the edge of the Church Shelf. He is of the Coombs blood, his aunt Sophronia was called in August, and he believes the bell is a curse that can be ended with a box of dynamite. On 29 October he means to recover his sunk cargo from the bare Shelf and blow the drowned church to pieces. Wrong rite: it would bury the doors.

Verna Tibbetts, 31, Clyde's 'widow': she held Clyde on the shore through the ringing of 31 August until the tide turned; two nights later he rowed out to the Bonne Chance and left his swamped dory and his boots on the Point, to escape $1,400 he owed Galen Coombs and collect $2,000 from Merrymeeting Life. She has hired a Boston medium to raise his 'spirit' in a seance, to convince Galen and the island he is dead. She is frightened, not wicked, and she knows the bell's third rule better than anyone alive except Orpha and Peleg.
The Reverend Kingsley Trask, 29: stopped the ringing in July. He did not know. He blames himself for every death since, and he raised the money for the bell in the crate.

Hezekiah Sprague, Seth Wyman, Jabez Coombs, Reuben Farr and Eliphalet Tibbetts, the five Proprietors of 1871, all long dead: the ones who did it. Their reasons were the oldest reasons there are, fear for their own and a living to protect, and they were wrong, and they knew it by morning.
redHerrings: Rum-runners did it. The Coast Guard and the Rockland waterfront think the 'drownings' are Galen Coombs's men drowning informers or rivals and dressing it as an island ghost story. Galen's boats are out on dark nights and his men do sink things off the Point. He did not drown anyone; his own aunt was nearly taken.

Insurance fraud. Len Garrity's company suspects all three claims; Clyde Tibbetts really is a fraud, and alive on the Bonne Chance. The other three taken are really dead, and are sitting in the drowned church.

Sleepwalking, liquor, the grippe, 'sea fever'. Every rational explanation the Skeptic offers is worth hearing and one of them (Clyde) is true. A Physician can find nothing wrong with the called before or after.

Ardelia Vining is a vengeful ghost. She is not. She is the bell's ringer, still ringing for help; she is dangerous only to anyone who stands between her and the doors, and the Sensitive can feel that she is not angry, only cold and waiting. This is not a revenge story, and the dead do not want the families dead; they want to be let out and named.

The Point families' descendants want revenge. Mattie Grindle is angry and has every right to be, and the GM may let the islanders suspect her. She wants the truth said and the Point's fishing privileges back, not anyone harmed.
clues: A. THE BELL RINGS AT THE LOWEST NIGHT LOW WATER OF EACH SPRING TIDE (RULE 1). A1: Carrow Head Light's 1924 logbook: 'bell heard under water off Church Point' on 1 Aug, 16 Aug, 31 Aug, 15 Sept, 30 Sept, each time within twenty minutes of the night low water (db-scenario-001). A2: the tide table nailed by the Store telephone set against Len Garrity's claim file's dates and times (db-scenario-001). A3: Zeb Lunt's ringing book in the church tower, fifty-two years of dates, every one at a full or new moon low water (db-scenario-001). A4: the fishermen at the Store stove: 'She only rings on the big tides. Bottom of the tide. Never by day' (db-scenario-001). A5: the Reverend Joel Vining's 1872 letter to his brother, which the brother's daughter, an old woman in Rockland, still keeps in her writing desk (db-scenario-002).

B. IT CALLS ONLY THE BLOOD OF THE FIVE PROPRIETORS (RULE 2). B1: the church register and the Burying Ground stones: Enoch Farr, Esther Thurlow (mother a Tibbetts), Jotham Wyman, Sophronia Coombs, Clyde Tibbetts, and Philena Farr in 1898 were all of the five families (db-scenario-001). B2: Sophronia Coombs and Verna Tibbetts: the called hear their own family name in the bell, 'Coombs, Coombs, like Mother calling me in' (db-scenario-001). B3: Orpha Sprague's warning to Dr. Thurlow, to Peleg, to anyone of the blood: 'You keep off the shore on the big tides. You have the Tibbetts in you' (db-scenario-001). B4: the five signatures on the 1871 order (db-scenario-003 or 004). B5: the Sensitive's Thin Place at the shore during a ringing: the bell is calling 'the five', not the island (db-scenario-001 or 002). B6: the ballad's third verse, 'she calls them home by their fathers' names, the Farr and the Wyman sons, the Sprague and the Tibbetts and Coombs's blood, for the five that held the doors' (db-scenario-001, Thankful Lunt sings it to Imogen Lisle).

C. IT CAN BE ANSWERED, AND THE CALLED CAN BE HELD (RULE 3). C1: Joel Vining's bequest in the church's deed box: $400 'to ring the bell at the lowest night low water of every spring tide, by hand, so long as the old bell shall ring under the sea' (db-scenario-001). C2: 16 Aug: Peleg Sprague rang the church bell by hand and nobody was taken; Sophronia was found at the tide line, alive (db-scenario-001, from Peleg or Sophronia). C3: 31 Aug: Verna Tibbetts held Clyde on the shore until the tide turned and he came back (db-scenario-001, from Verna under pressure). C4: 30 Sept: the fog bell's clockwork ran through the low water and Jotham was taken anyway; 'by hand' matters (db-scenario-001, Oren Pinkham's log and Ellery's grief). C5: the ballad's second verse, 'ring her an answer, ring her by hand' (db-scenario-001).

D. THE CHURCH DOORS WERE SPIKED SHUT BY THE FIVE PROPRIETORS (THE TRUTH OF 1871). D1: Nehemiah Pinkham's 1871 logbook at the Light, 18 to 19 Oct: 'Bell at Point meeting house rang from 11 p.m. Five lanterns on the Bar. No boat put off. Bell ceased 3.40 a.m. Meeting house gone. God forgive this island' (db-scenario-001 or 002). D2: the board of health minute of 9 Oct 1871 in the town records at the Store: an order to 'remove the sick of the Point to the meeting house and keep them there' (db-scenario-001 or 002). D3: the doors themselves, seen on 29 Oct: eight iron spikes driven through the west doors from outside, and the windows boarded from outside (db-scenario-002). D4: the names and prayers scratched in the vestibule plaster with a nail, and 'THEY ARE ON THE BAR WITH LANTERNS' (db-scenario-002). D5: Orpha Sprague's confession (db-scenario-003 or 004). D6: the order itself, in the Sprague Bible (db-scenario-003 or 004). D7: the Hannah Leighton's owners' letter of inquiry in the Mariner, November 1871, asking why the crew were in a church on a point in a gale (db-scenario-002, Rockland).

E. IRON BARS THE DEAD (RULE 4). E1: the iron spike or horseshoe over almost every door in the Harbor, put up by grandfathers in 1872, 'for luck', and the old women who will not take theirs down (db-scenario-001). E2: the spikes on the church doors held them for fifty-three years; once drawn, the dead come ashore (db-scenario-002 and 003). E3: the Drowned stop and knock at doors with iron, and walk into houses without it (db-scenario-003). E4: Oren Pinkham: 'Nothing's ever come up the Head. It's an iron tower' (db-scenario-003). E5: Joel Vining's letter: 'They could not pass the iron, God help them, and so they cannot pass it now' (db-scenario-002).

F. HOW IT ENDS: OPEN THE DOORS, SPEAK THE NAMES, RING ONCE FOR EACH, BY THE FIVE'S BLOOD, BEFORE THE ISLAND (RULE 5). F1: the ballad's last verse, which Zeb Lunt never sang in public and wrote upside down inside the back cover of his ringing book: 'Oh, who'll draw the nails that the five men drove, and who'll call the names of the drowned? For she'll ring for the blood of the five men's sons till the last of the names is found' (db-scenario-001 or 002). F2: Joel Vining's letter: 'I believe she will be quiet only when one of their own blood rings for each of them by name, before all the island, so that the island owns what it did' (db-scenario-002). F3: Ardelia Vining herself, to the Sensitive, in the drowned church or in the storm: 'Say who we were. Say it where they can hear' (db-scenario-002 or 003). F4: the names: the order in the Sprague Bible (all twenty-three), the vestibule plaster (seventeen legible), the Hannah Leighton's crew list in the Mariner (six), the Burying Ground's cenotaphs (nine), Zeb Lunt's ringing book flyleaf (all twenty-three, Asahel Wyman and Philena Farr) (db-scenario-002 to 004). F5: the doors opened on 29 Oct end the call; the bell still rings on 13 Nov (db-scenario-002 and 004).

G. CLYDE TIBBETTS IS ALIVE. G1: his boots were left side by side above the tide line on the Point, dry inside, and the dory was swamped, not stove (db-scenario-001). G2: Verna Tibbetts has $300 in new Canadian banknotes in a sugar tin, and a letter postmarked Saint-Pierre (db-scenario-001). G3: Peg Tolman has seen a Carrow man called Clyde working on the deck of the Bonne Chance (db-scenario-001, Peg's backstory). G4: the seance: Pearl Haverty's script, mailed by Verna, describes 'Clyde's spirit' in detail; the real thing that comes is someone else (db-scenario-001). G5: Clyde himself, washed ashore alive from the Bonne Chance in the storm (db-scenario-003).

H. GALEN COOMBS MEANS TO BLOW UP THE DROWNED CHURCH. H1: forty sticks of dynamite bought in Rockland on the mail boat's freight list, consigned to 'G. Coombs, weir stakes' (db-scenario-002). H2: his men talk at the Grange dance: 'Galen says the big tide'll settle it, the bell and the cargo both' (db-scenario-002). H3: the salt-sack cache on the Shelf's edge, visible from the Light's gallery at a low spring tide, and Galen's chart with the church marked X (db-scenario-002). H4: Galen himself, to anyone of the blood he trusts: 'I'll not wait to be called like Sophie. I'll put it back in the sea where it came from' (db-scenario-002).
controlFile.theKeyClue: The players solve the bell when they stop asking what it is and start asking whom it calls and why. Everything turns on the lighthouse logbook: the keeper's father wrote down on the night of 18 October 1871 that there were five lanterns on the Bar and no boat put off, and the keeper's son can put that page next to the 1924 log and the tide table. Point the first scenario's clues A, B and C hard, so that the party can save a life on 14 October; let the drowned church on 29 October show them D with their own eyes; let the storm teach them E; and leave F for the last. If the party reaches the lowest tide without knowing what they are walking into, have Oren Pinkham put his father's logbook on the kitchen table and say nothing at all.
controlFile.outcomes: There is no single right ending, only consequences. THE BELL: it is laid only by Rule 5, the doors opened and the twenty-eight names rung before the island by the five families' blood. If that is done on 13 November, the bell rings once more on its own, a single deep stroke under the sea, and never again, and everyone present drops to 0 Dread; the dead are seen, by those who look, walking up the Bar in the dusk and gone. If the doors were never opened (the party failed on 29 October or Galen's dynamite buried them), a diver in the Sculpin Cove deep-sea dress can draw the spikes on 13 November in the dark, which is the hardest thing in the campaign. If the island will not say the names, the bell goes on calling one of the blood every spring tide, and the answering ringing must be done by someone, by hand, forever; a party that sets that up, and leaves, has saved lives and solved nothing, which is an honest ending. THE ISLAND: if the truth is said before the island, Orpha Sprague says it, or Ellery Wyman, or Peleg reads it, and the Point's fishing privileges are given back to the Point families' heirs, Mattie Grindle first; the island is poorer and, by spring, kinder. If it is said only to the party, the families keep their silence and their wharf. THE STRANGERS: Esther Thurlow's body comes home to Bangor if the party bring her out of the church; Merrymeeting Life pays on her, and on Enoch Farr and Jotham Wyman, and not on Clyde Tibbetts, who can be turned in, let go to Saint-Pierre with Verna, or made to come home and face Galen. Peg Tolman's whisky reaches Galen, the Coast Guard, or the bottom of the bay. Galen Coombs, if his dynamite is stopped, may become the man who raises the bell with his salvage gear on 13 November, which is the best thing he will ever do. THE EPILOGUE: whatever happens, the GM should end with the first snow on the spruce, the mail boat leaving in the fog, and the sound of the Head's fog bell, and, if it was laid, no other bell at all.
